lead: A coupler splits light into two or more arms, an isolator passes light one way only, a circulator sends light round a fixed 1→2→3 route, and a fiber Bragg grating reflects one wavelength and passes the rest. None needs electrical power. They set how much power a WDM node loses and how much one channel leaks into its neighbour.
prereq: You need: the WDM channel and its spacing (WDM concepts) and decibels of power ratio.

sections.h3: Couplers: sharing light with no power supply

blocks.text: A coupler takes light in at one port and shares it among two or more output ports; run backwards, it combines several inputs into one output. The fused biconical taper (FBT) coupler is made by twisting two single-mode fibers together, fusing the joint and stretching it into a taper. Over the fused length the cores lie so close that light leaks from one core into the other. A planar coupler does the same with waveguides on a silica chip.

Name the ports of a 2×2 coupler this way: ports 1 and 2 on the input side, ports 3 and 4 on the output side. Light enters at port 1 with power P<sub>in</sub>; P₃ and P₄ come out, and a tiny P₂ comes back out of port 2. Shapes include the 1×2 splitter, the 2×2 coupler and the N×N star that shares every input among all N outputs. Splitting costs power: an ideal 1×N splitter gives each arm P<sub>in</sub>/N, a splitting loss of 10 log₁₀ N dB (3.01 dB for N = 2, 15.05 dB for N = 32).

items: Coupling ratio CR = P₃/(P₃ + P₄) × 100 percent: the share of the total output that leaves port 3.
Excess loss = 10 log₁₀(P<sub>in</sub>/(P₃ + P₄)) dB: power lost inside the coupler, found by adding all outputs.
Insertion loss (1→3) = 10 log₁₀(P<sub>in</sub>/P₃) dB: loss from the input to one chosen output; it contains both the split and the excess loss.
Directivity = 10 log₁₀(P<sub>in</sub>/P₂) dB: how little light comes back out of the other input-side port. A good fused coupler gives 40 dB or more, which keeps echoes out of the link.

blocks.text: Put all powers in the same unit (mW or µW); the ratio inside the log has no unit.
A laser diode is disturbed by light reflected back into it: the returning wave pulls its wavelength and adds noise (see Semiconductor laser diodes). An isolator is the one-way valve that stops it.

An isolator is a polarizer, a Faraday rotator and a second polarizer set at 45° to the first. The Faraday rotator, a magneto-optic crystal in a magnetic field, turns the plane of polarization by 45°, so forward light passes the second polarizer. The key fact: the crystal turns the plane in the same sense, viewed from the lab, whichever way the light travels. Light reflected back from the fiber passes the 45° polarizer, turns another 45°, arrives at 90° to the first polarizer and is blocked.

A circulator is the three-port version: light in at port 1 leaves by port 2, in at port 2 leaves by port 3, and in at port 3 leaves by port 1. Because a circulator routes light instead of splitting it, no 3 dB is thrown away. That makes it the natural partner of a Bragg grating.

sections.h3: Fiber Bragg gratings and the add-drop node

blocks.text: A fiber Bragg grating is a short piece of fiber whose core refractive index rises and falls periodically along the axis with pitch Λ. The forward wave reflects weakly at every period. The reflections add in phase for one wavelength only, the Bragg wavelength.

blocks.where: λ<sub>B</sub> is the reflected Bragg wavelength (m); n<sub>eff</sub> is the effective index of the guided mode, about 1.45 in silica; Λ is the grating pitch (m). The factor 2 is the round trip: the reflection from one period must travel one pitch forward and one pitch back to stay in step.

blocks.text: All other wavelengths pass almost untouched, so in transmission the grating is a band-stop (notch) filter, with a stop band from a fraction of a nanometre to a few nanometres wide. A sharp start and stop of the index pattern produce side lobes: small unwanted reflection peaks just outside the main band, sitting on the neighbouring WDM channels. Apodization, tapering the modulation strength gradually to zero at both ends, removes them. Gratings also serve as gain-flattening filters and, with a chirped pitch, as dispersion compensators.

With two circulators the grating becomes an optical add-drop multiplexer. Channels λ1 to λ4 enter port 1 of circulator C1 and leave at its port 2 into the grating. The grating reflects λ2 back into C1 port 2, and C1 sends it out of port 3: this is the drop. λ1, λ3 and λ4 pass through the grating into port 2 of circulator C2 and leave at C2 port 3, the output line. A new signal on λ2 enters C2 port 1, leaves at C2 port 2 towards the grating, is reflected back into C2 port 2, and joins the through channels at C2 port 3: this is the add.

examples.question: A fused 2×2 coupler receives P<sub>in</sub> = 250 µW at port 1. Port 3 gives 118 µW, port 4 gives 112 µW, and 4.0 nW comes back out of port 2. (a) Find the coupling ratio. (b) Find the excess loss. (c) Find the insertion loss from port 1 to port 3 and to port 4. (d) Find the directivity. (e) Find the grating pitch that reflects 1550 nm in a fiber with n<sub>eff</sub> = 1.45.
steps: (a) Total output P₃ + P₄ = 118 + 112 = 230 µW. CR = 118/230 × 100 = 51.3 percent, so the coupler is close to 50:50.
(c) Insertion loss 1→3 = 10 log₁₀(250/118) = 10 log₁₀(2.1186) = 3.26 dB. Insertion loss 1→4 = 10 log₁₀(250/112) = 10 log₁₀(2.2321) = 3.49 dB.
(e) From λ<sub>B</sub> = 2 n<sub>eff</sub> Λ: Λ = λ<sub>B</sub>/(2 n<sub>eff</sub>) = 1550/(2 × 1.45) = 1550/2.90 = 534.5 nm.
Check: the insertion loss 1→3 splits into the share part 10 log₁₀(230/118) = 2.90 dB plus the excess loss 0.36 dB, and 2.90 + 0.36 = 3.26 dB.
examples.answer: CR = 51.3 percent, excess loss = 0.36 dB, insertion loss = 3.26 dB (to port 3) and 3.49 dB (to port 4), directivity = 47.96 dB, grating pitch = 534.5 nm.

traps: Dropping the factor 2 in λ<sub>B</sub> = 2 n<sub>eff</sub> Λ. Without it the pitch comes out double (1069 nm instead of 534.5 nm for 1550 nm).
Treating excess loss and insertion loss as the same number. Excess loss compares the total output with the input; insertion loss compares one port with the input.
Measuring the coupling ratio against the input power instead of the total output. CR is a share of what comes out: 118/230, not 118/250.
Swapping isolation and insertion loss on an isolator. Isolation is the large reverse attenuation (30 to 60 dB); insertion loss is the small forward penalty (0.5 to 1 dB).

Drawing an add-drop node with one circulator and feeding the add channel into its port 3. Light into port 3 goes to port 1, back towards the source; the add path needs the second circulator after the grating.

quiz.q: State the Bragg condition for a fiber grating and name each symbol.
quiz.a: λ<sub>B</sub> = 2 n<sub>eff</sub> Λ, where λ<sub>B</sub> is the reflected wavelength, n<sub>eff</sub> the effective mode index (about 1.45 in silica) and Λ the grating pitch.

quiz.q: Why does an isolator block the reverse path but pass the forward path, when the Faraday rotator turns light by 45° both ways?
quiz.a: The Faraday rotation has the same sense in the lab for both directions. Forward light leaves the rotator at 45° and the second polarizer, set at 45°, passes it. Reflected light starts at 45°, is turned another 45° to 90°, and meets the first polarizer crossed, so it is blocked.

quiz.q: A 1×2 coupler gets 2.0 mW at port 1; ports 3 and 4 each give 0.90 mW. Find the coupling ratio, the excess loss and the insertion loss to one port.
quiz.a: CR = 0.90/1.80 × 100 = 50 percent. Excess loss = 10 log₁₀(2.0/1.80) = 0.46 dB. Insertion loss = 10 log₁₀(2.0/0.90) = 3.47 dB.

quiz.q: A Bragg grating must reflect 1310 nm in a fiber with n<sub>eff</sub> = 1.447. Find the pitch.
An ideal 32 × 32 star coupler has 0.5 dB excess loss. What power reaches each output for 1 mW (0 dBm) at one input?
quiz.a: Splitting loss = 10 log₁₀ 32 = 15.05 dB. Total loss = 15.05 + 0.5 = 15.55 dB, so each output gets −15.55 dBm = 10<sup>−1.555</sup> mW = 27.9 µW.

quiz.q: Explain how two circulators and a Bragg grating form an add-drop multiplexer, and why a 2×2 coupler is a poorer choice.
quiz.a: Channels enter C1 port 1 and leave at port 2 into the grating; the grating reflects λ2, which returns to C1 port 2 and is dropped at port 3. The other channels pass the grating into C2 port 2 and leave at C2 port 3. The added λ2 enters C2 port 1, goes out of port 2, is reflected by the grating and leaves at C2 port 3 with the through channels. A 2×2 coupler splits every channel, losing at least 3 dB per pass, and sends part of every channel into the drop port, which adds crosstalk.

beyond: Not for the exam. Planar lightwave circuits now put couplers, splitters and switches on one silica or silicon chip. Fiber Bragg gratings also serve as strain and temperature sensors, because the pitch stretches with the fiber and the reflected wavelength shifts. Search for planar lightwave circuits and fiber Bragg grating sensors.

figure.caption: Top: the worked example’s coupler, with 250 µW in, 118 µW and 112 µW out and 4.0 nW back at port 2. Bottom: a grating of pitch 534.5 nm reflects λ2 = 1550 nm, so C1 drops λ2 at its port 3, the other channels pass to C2, and a new λ2 added at C2 port 1 is reflected by the grating and joins them at C2 port 3.
